topics: Keeping Count with Marks
We can keep track of things even without counting: make one mark for each thing, and strike out one mark when it comes back
Longest and Shortest Names, Starting and Ending Letters
The longest name is the one with the most letters and the shortest has the fewest
Letters in Number Names

Sorting Things into Groups
To sort, choose a rule and put every thing in one of the groups

items: We can keep track of things even without counting: make one mark for each thing, and strike out one mark when it comes back. Marks left over show what is still missing.
One mark = one thing
Strike out one mark for each thing that comes back
Marks left = things not back
Draw marks in bunches of 5 so they are easy to count

notes.h: Longest and Shortest Names, Starting and Ending Letters
items: The longest name is the one with the most letters and the shortest has the fewest. Count every letter; do not judge by how big the name looks.
Count every letter, one by one
Longest = most letters; shortest = fewest
Two names can be equally long
Names can be grouped by their starting or ending letter
A number name has letters we can count: 43 = forty three = 5 + 5 = 10 letters. A two-word name has the letters of the tens word plus the ones word.
Count the letters of each word and add
Longest names from 1 to 99: 73, 77, 78 (12 letters)
Bigger number does not mean longer name
To sort, choose a rule and put every thing in one of the groups. The same things can be sorted in many ways. Then we can count each group.
A rule makes the groups
Every thing goes in one group
The same things can be grouped in many ways
After sorting, count each group
Wrong: We cannot keep track of things if we do not know how to count. Right: One mark for one thing keeps track without any numbers
Wrong: A name written bigger or wider is longer. Right: Count the letters: Mahesh and Kartik both have 6
Wrong: A bigger number always has a longer name. Right: 17 (seventeen, 9 letters) has a longer name than 70 (seventy, 7 letters)
Wrong: There is only one right way to group things. Right: Teji and Jojo grouped the same cards in two different ways — both are right

sol_items: Deba and Deep cannot count. What can they do to know no...: They make one mark on the wall for every cow going out and strike one mark out for every cow coming back.
All marks were struck out. Did all cows come back?: Yes, every cow came back.
Two marks were left but no cows were outside. Why were ...: Two marks left means two cows were still missing, so they must look for them.
Make marks for Hemant: Cows: 7 bunches of 5 and 1 mark. Sheep: 4 bunches of 5 and 3 marks.
Find the two team captains (longest and shortest animal...: Read the names from the book; the most letters is the longest name, the fewest is the shortest.
Mahesh or Kartik: Both have 6 letters, so they are equal.

5 bunches of 5 and 3 marks

How many letters are in Mahesh?
Which is longer: Ravi or Rekha? By how many letters?
Rekha, by 1 letter
Names: Raj, Rani, Ravi, Meera. How many start with R? Which ends with a?
3 start with R. Rani and Meera end with i and a: Meera ends with a

topics: Cube, Cuboid, Cylinder, Cone and Sphere
Many things around us have one of five shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone or sphere

A shape has faces (flat or curved), edges where faces meet (straight or curved) and corners where edges meet

notes.h: Cube, Cuboid, Cylinder, Cone and Sphere
items: Many things around us have one of five shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone or sphere. A cube is a special cuboid. Toys and models are often made of more than one shape.
Five shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere
A cube is a special cuboid
Many toys are made of more than one shape — count each shape

notes.h: Faces, Edges and Corners of Shapes
items: A shape has faces (flat or curved), edges where faces meet (straight or curved) and corners where edges meet. These parts tell the five shapes apart.
Face = surface, edge = where faces meet, corner = pointed place where edges meet (a cone's tip is a corner too)
Sphere: no edges; cube and cuboid: only flat faces
Cylinder and cone: flat and curved faces
Opposite faces of a die add to 7

notes.h: Building and Describing Models with Shapes
items: We put shapes together to build models. We say where each shape is with on, on top of, under and between, and we build from the bottom up.
On, on top of, under, between tell where a shape is
Build bottom first, top last
Cones make good roofs; spheres roll, so they are hard to build on

Cubes join face to face to make new shapes: in a line they make a cuboid, piled up a tower, bent an L. A cube joined to a cuboid face to face, with the same width and height and in a straight line, makes a longer cuboid (otherwise a different shape).
Cubes in a line make a cuboid; cube + cuboid of the same width and height, face to face in a line, make a longer cuboid
Count cubes layer by layer, hidden ones too
3 cubes: line or L
Wrong: A cube is not a cuboid at all. Right: A cube IS a cuboid — a special one whose sides are all the same square
Wrong: A cylinder has only curved faces. Right: A cylinder has a curved face AND two flat round faces at the ends
Wrong: We can start building from the top shape. Right: The bottom shape goes first — the top shape needs something to rest on
Wrong: Joining two cubes makes a bigger cube. Right: Two cubes in a row make a cuboid — longer than it is wide

sol_items: Let us Play: Activity: one child builds, another describes with on, under, between.
Which shape do you find the most? The least?: Read from your own table.
Shapes with only flat faces: Cube and cuboid
Shapes with both straight and curved edges: None of the five has both kinds of edge; cylinder and cone have curved edges only.
Shapes with both flat and curved faces: Cylinder and cone
Which shapes can you build with clay and sticks?: Cube and cuboid (balls for corners, sticks for edges).

Cube
Name the shape of a cricket ball.

Cylinder at the bottom, cone on top

Cuboid most; cone least

intro: In Class 3 Maths Chapter 3, Double Century, the topics are: What is 100?, making 100 in different ways, estimating how many, hundreds, tens and ones, number names and number sentences up to 200, numbers 100 to 200 on the number line. topics: What is 100?
With only ten symbols, 0 to 9, we can write every number
Making 100 in Different Ways
100 can be split into two numbers in many ways: 70 and 30, 65 and 35, 45 and 55
Estimating How Many
To estimate is to make a good guess of how many by looking, without counting all
Hundreds, Tens and Ones
10 bundles of 10 make one bundle of 100
Number Names and Number Sentences up to 200
A number beyond 100 is said and written as 'one hundred' and the rest: 151 = 100 and 51 = One hundred and fifty one
Numbers 100 to 200 on the Number Line
On the number line, numbers stand in order, each one more than the one before

items: With only ten symbols, 0 to 9, we can write every number. One more than 99 is 100, and 100 is the same as 10 tens — 10 bundles of 10 sticks.
Ten symbols 0–9 write every number; 0 means nothing
One more than 99 is 100
100 = 10 tens = 10 bundles of 10
A century is 100 runs
100 can be split into two numbers in many ways: 70 and 30, 65 and 35, 45 and 55. We find the partner with bundles, a ginladi or jumps on a number line.
Tens numbers: the tens make 10 (60 and 40)
Other numbers: the ones make 10 and the tens make 9 (45 and 55)
0 and 100 also makes 100
To estimate is to make a good guess of how many by looking, without counting all. Then we count and see how close the estimate was.
Estimate → count → how close?
Use a group of 10 to guess bigger amounts
10 bundles of 10 make one bundle of 100. A number like 123 is 1 bundle of 100, 2 bundles of 10 and 3 loose sticks — 1 hundred, 2 tens and 3 ones.
1 bundle of 100 = 10 bundles of 10
Write hundreds, then tens, then ones
0 holds an empty place (104)

notes.h: Number Names and Number Sentences up to 200
items: A number beyond 100 is said and written as 'one hundred' and the rest: 151 = 100 and 51 = One hundred and fifty one. After 199 comes 200 = 2 hundreds.
151 = 100 and 51 = One hundred and fifty one
30 more than 150 = 180
200 = 2 hundreds = 20 tens
A number can be made in more than one way

notes.h: Numbers 100 to 200 on the Number Line
items: On the number line, numbers stand in order, each one more than the one before. We fill missing numbers, mark a number between two tens, jump in 5s and 20s, and find 1 less and 1 more.
1 less is just before, 1 more is just after
Find the two tens, then count small steps
Wrong: After 99 comes 'ten-ty' or 910. Right: 99 and one more makes 100 — 10 tens, written 1, 0, 0
Wrong: 45 and 65 makes 100 (adding 4 + 6 = 10 tens AND 5 + 5). Right: when the ones make a new ten, the tens need only 9 — 45 and 55
Wrong: An estimate must be exactly right. Right: an estimate is a good guess — close is good; counting gives the exact number
Wrong: 101 and 110 are the same — both have 1, 0, 1. Right: 101 = 1 hundred, 0 tens, 1 one; 110 = 1 hundred, 1 ten, 0 ones
Wrong: One hundred and fifty two is written 10052. Right: 100 and 52 is 152 — the 52 takes the tens and ones places
Wrong: One less than 160 is 150. Right: one less is just one step back: 159

sol_items: What is 100?: 100 is one more than 99, and 10 bundles of 10.
Make 100 with bundles: 80 and 20 makes 100. 50 and 50 makes 100.
Make 100: 60 and 40; 45 and 55; 75 and 25; 15 and 85.
Flower petals: Fill the petal with its partner to 100, as in 30 and 70.
Fill the table 101 to 110 (number and name): 101 one hundred and one, 102 one hundred and two, up to 110 one hundred and ten.
Fill the number lines 100 to 110 and 111 to 124: 100, 101, ... 110 and 111, 112, ... 124.
imp_items: What number comes after 99?
How many bundles of 10 sticks make 100?
Write the partner of 45 to make 100.
Write the partner of 28 to make 100.
Make 100 with a jump to the next ten: 63 and ?
There are 38 seeds. Anu guessed 30 and Ravi guessed 50. Who is closer?
Anu is closer (8 off against 12)

topics: Finding the Hidden Part
When we know the total and the part we can see, the hidden part is the total take away the seen part
Adding and Subtracting with a Tens Frame
A tens frame has 10 squares
Adding and Subtracting on a Ginladi
On a ginladi (a string of 100 beads in groups of 10) or a number line we add by jumping forward and subtract by jumping back or ...
Jumping on the Ginladi
Jumping by the same number again and again: when we jump by 10, the ones digit stays the same and the tens digit goes up (or ...
Adding and Subtracting on the Number Grid
On the 1–100 number grid one row up is +10 and one step right is +1 (one row down is −10, one step left is −1)
Magic Sums and Magic Squares
In a magic-sum puzzle each number 1–9 is used once; each row adds to the red number and each column to the blue number
Word Problems: Finding the Total
When two parts are put together, draw a box diagram with the two parts, then add — with bundles and sticks or on a number line

When the total and one part are known, the missing part = total − part
Estimating More or Less than 100
Before working out, change a number to an easy ten-number (80 + 20 = 100; 150 − 50 = 100) to say if the answer is more or less ...

items: When we know the total and the part we can see, the hidden part is the total take away the seen part. Seen part + hidden part = total.
Seen part + hidden part = total
Hidden part = total − seen part
Check by adding back: seen + hidden must give the total

notes.h: Adding and Subtracting with a Tens Frame
items: A tens frame has 10 squares. Fill one frame to make 10, then count the rest — so sums up to 20 are seen in one look.

notes.h: Adding and Subtracting on a Ginladi
items: On a ginladi (a string of 100 beads in groups of 10) or a number line we add by jumping forward and subtract by jumping back or counting up. Different jumps give the same answer.
Jumping by the same number again and again: when we jump by 10, the ones digit stays the same and the tens digit goes up (or down) by 1.

notes.h: Adding and Subtracting on the Number Grid
items: On the 1–100 number grid one row up is +10 and one step right is +1 (one row down is −10, one step left is −1). Add a two-digit number with row moves for its tens and steps for its ones.
Words for adding: more, added to, total, sum
Words for subtracting: take away, difference, less, reduce
In a magic-sum puzzle each number 1–9 is used once; each row adds to the red number and each column to the blue number. In a magic square every row, column and diagonal adds to 15.
Blue total = red total = 45, because both add all the numbers 1 to 9
Magic square: 5 in the middle, every line = 15
When two parts are put together, draw a box diagram with the two parts, then add — with bundles and sticks or on a number line. Ten loose sticks make one new bundle.

notes.h: Word Problems: Missing Part and How Many More
items: When the total and one part are known, the missing part = total − part. When two amounts are compared, how many more = bigger − smaller. Draw the box diagram first.
Before working out, change a number to an easy ten-number (80 + 20 = 100; 150 − 50 = 100) to say if the answer is more or less than 100; then check on a number line, which can start at any number.
Wrong: Add the two numbers you know: 15 and 12 make 27 hidden seeds. Right: 15 is already the total — take the seen 12 away: 3 are hidden
Wrong: After the frame is full, start counting again from 1. Right: a full frame is 10 — go on 11, 12, …
Wrong: To subtract you must always jump back. Right: you can also count up from the smaller number to the bigger — the jumps give the same answer
Wrong: Jumping 10 from 7 lands on 10, 20, 30. Right: 7 + 10 = 17, then 27, 37 … — the 7 stays in the ones place
Wrong: To add 11 you must make 11 single steps. Right: 11 = one row up (10) + one step (1)
Wrong: In every puzzle all rows add to the same number. Right: only in a magic square; in magic-sum puzzles each row has its own total

Total 27 seeds, 12 seen. How many hidden? Check by adding.

intro: In Class 3 Maths Chapter 5, Fun with Shapes, the topics are: Straight and Curved Lines in Shapes, flat shapes on the faces of boxes, square corners, rectangle, square, triangle, circle and its centre, building shapes with squares and matchsticks, comparing shapes: same and different. topics: Straight and Curved Lines in Shapes
Flat shapes are drawn with straight lines (square, rectangle, triangle) or with a curved line (circle)
Flat Shapes on the Faces of Boxes
When we trace a face of a box or open the box flat, we get flat shapes
Square Corners
All corners of a square and a rectangle are square corners
Rectangle
A rectangle has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners
Square
A square has 4 sides and 4 corners like a rectangle, but ALL its sides are equal
Triangle
A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners
Circle and Its Centre
A circle is a round shape made with one curved line
Building Shapes with Squares and Matchsticks
Squares join side by side to make new shapes and bigger rectangles
Comparing Shapes: Same and Different
We compare shapes by their sides, corners, lines and size

notes.h: Straight and Curved Lines in Shapes
items: Flat shapes are drawn with straight lines (square, rectangle, triangle) or with a curved line (circle). A rangoli or a saree border uses both.
Shapes with straight lines: square, rectangle, triangle
Shape with a curved line: circle

notes.h: Flat Shapes on the Faces of Boxes
items: When we trace a face of a box or open the box flat, we get flat shapes. The faces of a cuboid are rectangles or squares — never triangles.
A cuboid has 6 faces
Its faces are rectangles or squares
Opposite faces are the same
All corners of a square and a rectangle are square corners. A corner can be less than, equal to or more than a square corner — check with a paper strip or a book corner.
Square and rectangle: 4 square corners
Less / equal / more than a square corner
Book corner = tester
A rectangle has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners. Its opposite sides are equal in length.
4 sides, 4 corners
Opposite sides equal
All corners are square corners
A square has 4 sides and 4 corners like a rectangle, but ALL its sides are equal. Fold a square in half and you get a rectangle.
All 4 sides equal
4 square corners
Folded in half → a rectangle
A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. Triangles hide in many designs, and other shapes can be split into triangles.
3 sides, 3 corners
Turned triangles are still triangles
Count small ones first, then bigger ones
A circle is a round shape made with one curved line. It has no straight sides and no corners. Folding a circle in half two ways shows its centre.
Round, one curved line
No sides, no corners
Two half-folds meet at the centre

notes.h: Building Shapes with Squares and Matchsticks
items: Squares join side by side to make new shapes and bigger rectangles. Joined squares share sides, so they need fewer matchsticks.
Shared sides save sticks
Turned shapes are the same
Count missing squares by continuing the grid
We compare shapes by their sides, corners, lines and size. A shape can be turned, made bigger or smaller and still be the same shape.
Compare sides, corners, lines, size
Turning or resizing keeps the shape
Wrong: A line that turns at a corner is a curved line. Right: At a corner two straight lines meet; a curved line bends smoothly all along and has no corner
Wrong: A box has 6 different faces. Right: Opposite faces of a box are the same — a cuboid has at most 3 different faces
Wrong: Every corner is a square corner. Right: Many corners are less or more than a square corner — test with a book corner
Wrong: A tilted rectangle is not a rectangle. Right: Turning a rectangle does not change its sides and corners
Wrong: A tilted square is a diamond, not a square. Right: Turning does not change it: 4 equal sides and 4 square corners
Wrong: A triangle must stand on its flat side. Right: A turned or upside-down triangle is still a triangle — count its sides

sol_items: Make Amma rangoli on the dots: Activity: join the dots part by part.
Make a boat, a butterfly and a rocket with cut-out: Activity: for example a boat from a triangle sail and a rectangle base.
Open cardboard boxes: Rectangles and squares.
Faces of a TV, a box and a chocolate: The faces are rectangles.
Why did the two children get different shapes (wooden b...: The two boxes have faces of different sizes and shapes.
Trace faces of a cuboid: how many different faces and t...: At most 3 different faces; all are rectangles (or squares). No face is a triangle. A cuboid has 6 faces, each rectangle or square.

Circle
Sort square, circle, triangle, rectangle: straight lines or curved line.
Straight: square, triangle, rectangle. Curved: circle.
Can a face of a cuboid be a triangle? Name the faces.
No; rectangles or squares
How many faces does a cuboid have?
A rectangle has ___ sides and ___ corners.
4 and 4
How is a square different from a rectangle?
All four sides of a square are equal

title: House of Hundreds - I
intro: In Class 3 Maths Chapter 6, House of Hundreds - I, the topics are: Counting Beyond 200, hundreds, tens and ones, 3-digit numbers on a number line, house numbers and number patterns, comparing 3-digit numbers. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Counting Beyond 200
Big collections are counted in tens first (10, 20 … 200, 210 …) and then the loose ones are counted on
Hundreds, Tens and Ones
10 ones make 1 ten and 10 tens make 1 hundred
3-Digit Numbers on a Number Line
On a number line numbers grow as we go right
House Numbers and Number Patterns
In a house-number grid each floor has 10 houses
Comparing 3-Digit Numbers
To compare, look at the hundreds first; if they are the same, look at the tens; if those are the same too, look at the ones

items: Big collections are counted in tens first (10, 20 … 200, 210 …) and then the loose ones are counted on. After 299, one more makes 300 — the next hundred.
Count big collections in tens, then count on the loose ones
After 200 the names repeat: two hundred and ten, two hundred and twenty …
To find how many more to 300, count on in tens
10 ones make 1 ten and 10 tens make 1 hundred. A 3-digit number tells how many hundreds, tens and ones it has: 235 = 2 hundreds, 3 tens, 5 ones = 200 + 30 + 5.
10 ones = 1 ten; 10 tens = 1 hundred
0 holds a place when there are no tens or no ones
Adding 10 changes the tens; adding 1 changes the ones
On a number line numbers grow as we go right. Read the jump between the marks, find the two marks a number lies between, then count on. Jumps show how far one number is from another.
Numbers grow to the right
Read the jump between marks first
Find the two marks the number lies between
Jump to the next ten, then by tens, to find how far
In a house-number grid each floor has 10 houses. One house right is 1 more, one floor up is 10 more. So any house number can be found without counting.
Each floor has 10 houses
Right = 1 more, left = 1 less
Up = 10 more, down = 10 less
Up and right = 11 more; down and right = 9 less

To compare, look at the hundreds first; if they are the same, look at the tens; if those are the same too, look at the ones. Write > for 'is more than' and < for 'is less than' — the open side faces the bigger number.
Hundreds first, then tens, then ones
A 3-digit number is more than any 2-digit number
> is more than, < is less than; the open side faces the bigger number
Greatest: biggest digit in hundreds; smallest: smallest digit in hundreds
Wrong: After 299 comes 2100 (or 2910). Right: 299 and one more is 300 — the next hundred
Wrong: 301 and 310 are the same — both have a 3, a 0 and a 1. Right: 301 has 1 loose stick; 310 has 1 bundle of ten — the place of the digit changes its value
Wrong: Every gap on a number line is 1. Right: Read the marks: the gap can be 1, 10, 50 or 100
Wrong: One floor up is 1 more. Right: One floor up is 10 more (105 → 115); one house right is 1 more
Wrong: 209 is more than 290 because it has a 9 at the end. Right: That 9 is 9 ones; 290 has 9 TENS — 209 < 290

sol_items: Jojo has 2 toffees in his hand: The count of the boxes plus 2.

topics: Multiplication as Equal Groups

The same things can be put into equal groups in different ways; the total does not change

Multiplying Bigger Numbers

items: When every group has the same number of things, we can add that number again and again, say it as 'times' and write it with ×: 5 groups of 2 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 5 times 2 = 5 × 2 = 10.
Equal groups → add the same number again and again
First number = how many groups, second = how many in each group
The same things can be put into equal groups in different ways; the total does not change. 8 groups of 6 and 6 groups of 8 are both 48, so 8 × 6 = 6 × 8.

Skip jumping = jumping the same number of steps every time from 0. The number reached after some jumps is jumps × jump size, so skip jumps make the times tables.
Number reached = number of jumps × jump size
Jump size = gap between two neighbours

Times tables from 1 × 1 to 10 × 10 can be made by sticks, skip jumps or repeated addition. Tables have patterns: times-5 answers end in 5 or 0, and the table of 2 plus the table of 3 gives the table of 5.
Tables can be built by sticks, jumps or adding
Times-5: 0 or 5 at the end
Tables add: 2-table + 3-table = 5-table

Division splits a total into equal groups. It answers 'how many does each get?' (18 laddoos among 9 → 2 each) or 'how many groups can we make?' (12 wheels, 2 per cycle → 6 cycles). We write 18 ÷ 9 = 2.

Share one by one, round after round, until nothing is left

Break the big number into 10s and ones
Multiply each part, then add the parts
To divide a bigger number, take away the group size again and again (or a big chunk of groups at once) and count how many times you took it away. Anything smaller than one group is left over.
Subtract the group size again and again; count the subtractions
Take 10 groups at a time to be faster
Smaller than one group at the end = left over

topics: Fair Sharing: Equal or Not?
A share is fair only when every share is exactly the same size
What Is a Half?
When 1 whole is shared equally between 2 people, each share is called a half
Half and Double
Half of a number of things = share them equally into 2 groups and take one group
What Is a Quarter?
When a whole is shared equally among 4 people, each share is called a quarter
Half or Quarter?
For a group of things: share them into 2 equal groups → one group is half; share into 4 equal groups → one group is a quarter

items: A share is fair only when every share is exactly the same size. We check by putting one piece over the other (folding) — equal pieces match exactly.
Fair share = equal share
Fold or put one piece on top of the other to check
Share things one to each in turn
When 1 whole is shared equally between 2 people, each share is called a half. Two halves make one whole, and a half can be made in many different ways.
Half = each share when 1 whole is shared equally between 2 people (say 'one half')
2 halves make 1 whole
Many ways to make a half
Say 'one half', not '1 out of 2'
Half of a number of things = share them equally into 2 groups and take one group. Double = the number added to itself. 3 is half of 6, so 6 is double of 3.
Half: share into 2 equal groups
Double: add the number to itself
If a is half of b, then b is double of a
When a whole is shared equally among 4 people, each share is called a quarter. Four quarters make one whole; a quarter is half of a half.
Quarter = each share when 1 whole is shared equally among 4 people (say 'one quarter', one fourth or half of half)
4 quarters = 1 whole
Quarter = half of half (also one fourth)
For a group of things: share them into 2 equal groups → one group is half; share into 4 equal groups → one group is a quarter. Half of a group is double a quarter of it.
Half of a group: 2 equal groups
Quarter of a group: 4 equal groups
Half is double of a quarter
Count quarters to the whole: 1 quarter, 2 quarters (= half), 3 quarters (three-quarters), 4 quarters (= the complete whole). Quarters must be equal in size, but they may have different shapes.
1, 2, 3, 4 quarters
2 quarters = half; 4 quarters = whole
Three-quarters = whole minus one quarter
Equal size, any shape
Wrong: Any two pieces are a fair share. Right: Two pieces are fair only if they are the same size — check by putting one on the other

Wrong: Double means add 2 (double of 6 = 8). Right: Double means add the number to itself: 6 + 6 = 12
Wrong: Any 4 pieces are quarters. Right: The 4 pieces must be equal — the paratha cut into 4 unequal pieces does not show quarters
Wrong: A quarter always means 4 things. Right: A quarter of 8 is 2, a quarter of 16 is 4 — share into 4 equal groups and count one group
Wrong: 3 coloured parts always show three-quarters. Right: Only if the whole has 4 EQUAL parts — 3 of 5 parts is not three-quarters

topics: Hundreds, Tens and Ones

Different Ways of Making a Number
One number can be made in many ways: as hundreds, tens and ones, as a sum (300 + 60 + 8), as 'more than' a hundred or 'less than' ...

Number Line
On a number line the marks go up by the same jump

notes.h: Different Ways of Making a Number
items: One number can be made in many ways: as hundreds, tens and ones, as a sum (300 + 60 + 8), as 'more than' a hundred or 'less than' the next hundred, or by any number sentence that gives it.

Read the cards left to right like digits

When we cannot count everything, we estimate: we decide which range a quantity lies in (0–10, 11–50 … more than 1000) by thinking of something we know.

Choose the range that fits

Before the knot = less
At the knot = equal
Same floor, same start

2 halves = 1 metre
4 quarters = 1 metre

topics: Which Vessel Holds More?

notes.h: Filling a Big Vessel with Small Vessels
items: We can measure how much a big vessel holds by counting how many times a small vessel is poured into it. A big vessel can also fill many small ones — the amount stays the same.

We compare weights by holding things in both hands or on a pan-balance: the heavier thing pulls the hand or the pan down. A big thing is not always heavy.

kg = the weight everyone agrees on.

Add or subtract the hundreds to get the estimate
Estimate first, then calculate, then check they are close

items: A month calendar shows every date of the month under its day of the week. Seven columns are the seven days; going down a column, the date grows by 7.

Same day of the week → dates jump by 7
Count on from a date to find a date some days later

notes.h: Months and Days in a Year
items: A year has 12 months and 365 days, which is 52 weeks and 1 day. The names of months and the 7 days of a week never change, but the day on which a date falls, and some festival dates, change from year to year.
12 months, 365 days in a year
52 weeks and 1 day in a year
February is the only month with less than 30 days

Age is the time passed since the date of birth. A birth certificate gives the date of birth as day/month/year; from it we find age in years, months or days. Two people's age gap stays the same all their lives.
Date = day/month/year
Age = later year − birth year (on or after the birthday)
The age gap between two people never changes
An analog clock has a short hour hand and a long minute hand. The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows minutes — each number it points to means 5 minutes more.
Short = hour, long = minute
Number × 5 = minutes
Long hand on 12 = o'clock
Time taken = from the start time to the end time. Count how many 5-minute jumps the long hand makes; one full round of the long hand is 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Count jumps of 5 from start to end
Full round of the long hand = 60 minutes = 1 hour
A digital clock shows time with digits; an analog clock shows it with hands. A sand clock does not show the time of day — it measures how long something takes.
Digital = digits
Analog = hands
Sand clock = timer
Different things take different amounts of time. Short things are measured in minutes, longer ones in hours, days, weeks, and very long ones in months.
minutes < hours < days < weeks < months
